newsitem.title: UK: Palladium premium up on tight supply, Russia cited.
newsitem.headline: Palladium premium up on tight supply, Russia cited.

text.p: Premiums for favoured grades of palladium are rising due to tightness in supply caused by stalled Russian exports.
A delayed start to Russian negotiations with Japanese importers resulted from an apparently ongoing reallocation of the responsibilities for the export of platinum group metals (PGMs) from Russia.
"The shortfall looked artificial last year but palladium has been tightening and the price is moving up," a dealer said.
So is the premium for the more highly refined sponge grade material used in electronics and increasingly in autocatalysts to remove toxic gases from vehicle exhaust fumes.
The shortage has forced consumers to seek material in the dealer market and attracted speculator buying as well.
Palladium was indicated at $127.25/$128.25 per ounce on Thursday having fixed at $128.00 earlier in the week, its highest fix since August 14, 1996.
The price has been rising steadily since it fell to its lowest level since April 16, 1993 on November 28 last year to $114.25.
Demand for palladium-bearing goods like electronics has been booming again in Japan ahead of an increase in a domestic sales tax due in April.

That is in sharp contrast to last year when Japanese imports were sharply lower than in 1995 as the electonics and car makers found themselves caught by the Japanese economic turndown with high stocks of raw materials and components.
According to official statistics in the first 10 months of last year 66.26 tonnes of palladium were imported versus 85.01 tonnes in the same 1995 period. More than 85 percent came from Russia.
"There are real signs that the Japanese palladium users worked through their inventories last year," a market analyst specialising in PGMs said.
Russia is traditionally producer and exporter of ingot grade palladium which is used in dental alloys and is less easily adapted to the higher technology uses filled by sponge.
"The Russians have been producing some sponge recently but as most of the exports last year were from stockpiles, they were mainly in ingot form," a dealer said.
He said there was a surge in Russian shipments to the United States late last year.
"It is not clear why this happened. Maybe they forecast problems with the negotiations but (U.S.) import statistics were very high in November," a dealer said.
Another platinum group observer suggested that members of the Almazjuvelirexport (Almaz) export licensing agency simply signed more licences than usual before the export process was restructured.
Nevertheless, the higher export eased growing supply tightness and prevented the price going higher -- despite being in the less favoured ingot form.
"What has happened is that the premium of sponge over ingot has risen to reflect the market tightness although these shipments kept the base price lower than it could have been," the dealer said.
Premiums for sponge have stretched to over $3.00 per ounce from about half of that last month.
Most of the shortage of sponge has been in the U.S. where technology is geared to its use.
Dealers said some ingot was being "grained" to substitute for sponge grade.
"It doesn't work for everything, it depends on the fabricator," a dealer said. "Graining can alleviate part of the problem but it doesn't solve it all."
Also stalling talk was the fact that Russia's budget was not agreed by the lower house of parliament until January 24 and the upper house is not due to pass it until February 12.
Dealers forecast that even if talks began immediately after budget approval it would be April before contracted shipments could begin.
Traditionally, exports have been priced on a monthly average basis meaning this year, the first average price available would be from March.
Dealers also speculated that once administrative problems were sorted out, Russia could beginning export to the spot market immediately.
Alternatively it might try to catch up on lost first quarter shipments by asking some or all of its 13 Japanese counterparties to accept twice as much metal as contracted in the first few months.
"Normally the previous year's contract would just have been rolled over into the next year if there was a problem," a dealer said.
"But with the administrative changes this time nobody knew what was happening so that was not possible, apparently," he added.
